Setting up of growth centres in the backward areas of U.P. 
†*381. SHRI MANOHAR KANT DHYANI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a scheme'was approved by Government for the setting up 
of growth centres in the backward areas; 
(b) if so, whether approval has been accorded to all the growth centres to be set up in 
U.P.; 
(c) the status of the growth centre approved for Kotdwar district of Pauri Garhwal 
and by when it is likely to start functioning; and 
(d) the amount which has, so far, been provided to Uttar Pradesh in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Central Government brought into operation in 1991 the Growth 
Centre Scheme for setting up Growth Centres in backward areas. The objective of the 
Scheme is to provide industrial infrastructure to enable these areas to attract industrial 
units. 
(b) and (c) Seven of the eight Growth Centres allotted to Uttar Pradesh have been 
approved by the Central Government. For the remaining one Growth Centre proposed 
to be set up in Distt. Pauri Garhwal, the State has yet to finalise the site and submit its 
detailed project report for approval by the Central Government. 
(c) Central release amounting to Rs. 2220 lakhs have been provided under this Scheme 
to Uttar Pradesh.

*388. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the impact of globalisation on the domestic industry, agriculture and  
employment in the country; and 
(b) what is the basis of Government's findings and conclusions in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The impact of globalization on domestic industry, agriculture and 
employment in the country has been analyzed in various issues of Economic Survey, Plan 
Documents of Planning Commission and other reports of the Government. The 
summary conclusions which emerge from these reports reveal the following: 
* Globalization and economic liberalization has enhanced competition, increased 
economic efficiency and augmented productivity of the domestic industry. As a 
result the industrial sector which recorded an average annual compound growth 
rate of 4.6% from 1970-71 to 1979-80 and 6.6% from 1980-1981 to 1989-90 
achieved a high growth rate of 7.3% in Eighth Plan (1992—97).

In the pre-reform period the agricultural sector had grown at the rate of 3.16 per 
annum from 1981-82 to 1985-86 and at the rate of 3.59% per annum from 1985-86 
to 1989-90. In the post reform period however, the agricultural sector has 
registered a higher growth rate of about 3.9% during the Eighth plan period 
(1992-97). 
The average annual growth rate of overall employment (both organized 
        or unorganized  sectors) after continuously declining   from 2.75% in 
          the period 1972—78 to 1.77% in 1983—1988, but increased to 2.37%  
            in the period 1987—1994.  
Thus the broad trends of growth in the post reform period indicate that the 
impact   of globalization on domestic industry, agriculture and employment 
have been by and large positive.

Study on the Progress of Literacy Among SC/ST Women 
*382. SHRI ANANTA SETHI: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have made country-wide study on the progress of literacy 
among SC/ST women; 
(b) if so, when was the last study made; 
(c) whether it is a fact that literacy rate has not improved substantially in the States like 
Orissa, Bihar and M.P.; 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether any special scheme is proposed to be implemented in those States to 
raise the literacy rate of SC/ST women; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) and (b) Although 
no country-wide study ont he progress of literacy among SC/ST women has been made, 
data regarding the progress of literacy among SC/ST communities are collected and 
published by the Census Commissioner of India on the basis of Census operations 
conducted every ten years. The last Census operatiosn were undertaken in 1991. 
(c) and (d) There has been substantial improvement in the rate of literacy in the Stats 
of Orissa Bihar and M.P., as shown in the statement attached (See below). 
(e) and (f) In order to raise the literacy rate of SC/ST women, Government is 
implementing the following schemes: 
(i) Educ, tional Complex in Low Literacy Pockets for Development of Women 
Literacy in Tribal Areas. 
Districts where literacy among ST women is less than 10% are covered under the 
scheme. A total 136 Districts in 11 Stat es, viz. Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Tamil 
Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal ta'' within the purview of the scheme. Full 
financial assistance is provided by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs for setting up 
of such Educational Complexes. 
24 

[21 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Ashram Schools on Tribal Sub-Plan Area 
The objective of the scheme is to  extend educational facilities like 
establishmentof residential schools for Scheduled Tribes in an environment 
conducive to learning. The funding for the scheme with the States is done on 
matching (50:50) basis, while 100% Central assistance is given to U.Ts. The Central 
assistance under the scheme is mainly for construction of Ashram School 
buildings, hostels and staff quarters. 
(iii) Girls Hostels for Scheduled Tribes 
The scheme is an useful instrument for spreading education among ST girls, 
under the scheme, Central assistance is given to States/UTs. for construction of 
new hostel buildings and/or extension of existing hostel buildings. While in the 
case of States the cost of construction is equally shared between the Centre and 
the States, full assistance is given by the Central Government to UTs. 
(iv)  Grant-in-aid to Voluntary Organizations working for the Welfare ofSTs. 
Under this scheme, grant-in-aid is given to Voluntary organisatiosn working 
for the welfare of STs for a wide spectrum of projects, including residential 
school hostels. balwadis.  
(v)  Special Educational Development programme Scheduled Caste Girls   be
 longing to very low literacy level.  
The scheme was introduced during 1996-97 on pilot basis with a view to provide 
a package of educational inputs through residential school for SC girls in areas 
of very low SC female literacy where traditions and environments are not 
conducive to their learning. The scheme is implemented by the Zila Parishads 
(district Level Panchayats). 48 Districts situated in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, 
Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh where the percentage of literate SC girls is less than 
2% as per 1981 census are eligible to take advantage of the scheme. 
(vi)  Girls Hostels for Scheduled Castes 
The main objective of the scheme is to  provide hostel facilities to SC girl 
students studying in middle schools, higher secondary schools, colleges and 
Universities, under the scheme, financial assistance is provided to State 
Governments on 50:50 matching share basis (100% to UTs) for construction of 
hostel buildings and other facilities. 
(vii) Grant-in-aid to Voluntary Organizatio ns working for the welfare of Scheduled 
Castes 
Under this scheme, govt. aid is given to voluntary organizations 
working for the welfare of SCs for various projects, including establishing 
schools and hostels to students belonging to SCs and for running balwadis and 
bal kendras.

Visit of German Delegation to India 
*386. SHRIBRAHMAKUMAR BHATT: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a delegation from Germany visited India; 
(b) whether the delegation agreed to participate in Information Technology 
and other areas; 
(c) if so, the details of the proposals; and 
(d) the details of the agreement signed? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) to (d) No delegation from Germany visited India to discuss 
specifically the bilateral cooperation in the information technology sector. 
However, a delegation led by Mr. Guenter Eymael, Secretary, Ministry of 
Economic Transportation, Agriculture and Viniculture in Rheinland Pfalz, 
Mainz, Germany visited the Ministry of Information Technology on 28th January 
2000 and had a discussion on the capabilities of Indian information technology 
and electronics industry including the sc ope for enhancemen t of bilateral 
cooperation. 
Mr. Joschka Fischer, Deputy Chancellor and Federal Minister for Foreign 
Affairs of the Federal Republic of Germany also visited India during May 
17-18,2000 during which he visited the Information Technology Park in Bangalore 
on 17th May, 2000. The delegation also held detailed discussions with the 
Indo-German Chamber of Commerce on measures for utilizing the potential for 
bilateral cooperation. 
No agreement has so far been signed between the two countries for 
cooperation in the information and technology sector.

THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AN D INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) to (c) Import restriction on 894 items (at 8 digit level) were removed on 
31.03.99 and the restrictions on 714 items (at 8 digit level) have been removed on 
31.03.2000. The notifications containing details of the commodities, on which QRs have

India has been following a continuous policy of removal of import restrictions since

seeks to convert all non-tariff barriers such  as, Quantitative Restrictions (QRS), into

apply tariffs within the bound level. In the case of India tariffs for primary agricultural

Protecting traditional system and biodiverse materials 
2973. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any attempt has been made to protect traditional system and biodiverse 
materials especially in the field of medicine; 
(b) whether it is a fact that on the issue of intellectual property rights fresh 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2000] 
obligations are sought to be imposed under the TRIPS agreement especially in the area of 
biotechnology and biodiverse materials; and 
(c) if answer to part (b) be in the affirmative then what steps Government are taking 
to make a combined campaign alongwith other developing and biodiverse materials 
producing countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) A task force, constituted to work out the modalities to 
document the traditional knowledge of Ay urveda in the form of a Traditional 
Knowledge Digital Library in order to prevent patenting of traditional knowledge, has 
submitted its report. Its implementation is under consideration of the Government. 
The Government has introduced the Biological Diversity Bill, 2000 in the Lok Sabha 
on 15 May, 2000. The broad objectives of this legislation are conservation and 
sustainable utilisation of biodiversity and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of the 
use of biological resources and knowledge. 
In order to protect bio-resources, the Patents (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999 
contains provisions for mandatory disclosure of source and geographical origin of the 
biological material used in the invention while applying for patents in India. Provisions 
have also been incorporated to include the nondisclosure or wrongful disclosure of the 
same as grounds for opposition and for revocation of the patent, if granted. Provisions in 
this regard are contained in clauses 8, 17 and 28 of the said Bill. 
In order to protect traditional knowledge from being patented, provisions have been 
incorporated in the Patents (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999, to include anticipation of 
invention by available local knowledge, including oral knowledge, as one of the grounds for 
opposition as also for revocation of patent. Provisions in this regard are contained in 
clauses 17 and 28 of the said Bill. 
(b) There has been no amendment to the TRIPs Agreement since it was adopted in 
1994 as a part of the Uruguay Round Agreement. 
(c) Does not arise. 
Liberalisation of FDI policy 
2974. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of decision taken for liberalisation of FDI policy; 
68 

[21 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the safeguards proposed to protect domestic industry; and 
(c) the total foreign exchange likely to be earned by allowing 100 per cent FDI in 
E-Commerce and removing exports obligations in consumer goods? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) Government, in its commitment towards economic 
reforms and with the objective of attracting more foreign direct investment has placed 
all items/activities under the automatic route for 100% Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), 
Non-Resident Indians (NRI) and Overseas Corporate Body (OCB) investment except 
the following: 
1. All proposals that require an Industrial Licence which include (i) the item 
requiring an Industrial Licence under the Industries (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 195 l;(ii) foreign investment being more than 24% in the equity 
capital of units manfuacturing items reserved for small scale industries; and 
(iii) all items which require an Industr ial Licence in terms of the locational 
policy notified by Government under the New Industrial Policy of 1991. 
2. All proposals in which the foreign collaborator has a previous venture/ tie-up in 
India. 
3. All proposals relating to acquisition of share in an existing Indian company in 
favour of a foreign/NRI/OCB investor. 
4. All proposals falling outside notified sectoral policy/caps or under sectors in 
which FDI is not permitted and/or whenever any investor chooses to make an 
application to the FIPB and not to avail of the automatic route. 
Government has further permitted FDI upto 100% in oil refinery and Business 
to.business e-commerce, removed the upper limit of FDI under automatic route for 
electric generation, transmission and distri bution (except Atomic power plants), and 
done away with the dividend balancing condition in respect of 22 consumer goods 
industries, since this condition was perceived by the foreign investors as an irritant. 
(b) FDI is not considered a threat to an efficient domestic industry. However, 
while considering FDI proposals, a declartion is obtained from the applicant 
whether the foreign collaborator has any previous joint venture or technology 
transfer/trademark agreement in the same or allied field in India, the detailed 
circumstances in which in is 
69 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2000] 
considered necessary to set up a new joint venture/enter into new technology 
transfer (including trade mark), and proof that the new proposal would not in 
any way jeopardise the interest of the existing joint venture or technology/trade 
mark partner or other stake holders. For induction of Foreign/NRI/OCB equity 
in an existing Indian company, a copy of the Board Resolution of the Indian 
company is called for. 
(c) The measures have been undertaken with the objective of attracting more FDI 
to the country and making India a more attractive investment destination. It is 
difficult to forecast the exact amount of FDI inflow on account of these 
measures, as investment by the foreign investors depends upon their 
commercial judgement and factors like availablity of adequate infrastructure.

(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) No Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) Government decides to disinvest its equity , partly or fully, in Public Sector 
Enterprises in accordance with the declared disinvestment policy. As stated in the 
budget speech for 2000-2001, the disinvestment policy of the Government applicable to

share to 26% is not automatic and the manner and pace of doing so is worked out on a

is aggreed to, however, the actual timing of disinvestment in a company depends on 
various factors like market conditions, financial performance of the company, terms and 
conditions of sale, interest shown by the investors/buyers and advice of the advisors to 
the Government.

Exposure of Vulgarity in TV Programmes 
2998. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have devised or propose to devise any method to check 
exposure of vulgarity in the programmes aired through foreign TV channels; and 
(b) what action Government have taken and whether they propose to set up a tribunal 
or judicial body for timely detection and prosecution of such channels? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING AND THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW, 
JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ARUN JAITELY): (a) and 
(b) The distribution through cable television networks of programmes of foreign 
satellite TV channels is governed by the provisions of the Cable Television 
networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and rules made thereunder. As per Section 
5 and 6 of the Cable Television networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, no cable 
operator shall transmit or retransmit any programme or advertisement on his 
cable service, unless these are in conformity with the prescribed codes. However, 
free to air programmes of foreign satellite channels are exempted from this 
provision. Enforcement of these provisions are to be done by the authorized 
officers to be notified by the respective State Governments. Some of the State 
Governments have not notified authorised officers for purposes of all the 
90 

[21 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
sections of the Act. Government has intr oduced a Cable TV Networks (Regulation) 
Amendment Bill in the current session of Parliament with a view to remove, amongst 
others, these lacuna. 
Further, the TV channels uplinking their programmes from India are bound through 
appropriate licensing conditions, to abide by the programme and advertisement codes as 
applicable to Doordarshan. However, the Government is not in a position to impose such 
conditions or obligations on the TV channels uplinking their programmes from outside 
the country, as they are not bound to seek permission or approval for downlinking. This 
situation has got further accentuated as these channels were earlier not permitted to 
uplink their programmes from India. In order to remove this anomaly, the Government 
has liberalized its uplinking policy recently enabling these channels to uplink their 
programmes from India,, so as to bring them within the ambit of our rules and regulations 
particularly, the ones relating to the compliance with our programme and advertisement 
codes. 
Government is also contemplating to bring a comprehensive legislation with a view, 
amongst others, to provide for regulation of broadcasting servicer including foreign 
satellite TV channels.

Constitutional provision for reservation to SCs/STs in recruitment and 
promotion 
3043. DR. (Ms.) P. SELVIE DAS:  
            SHRI GANDHI AZAD: 
Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any special provision in the Constitution for SCs/STs providing 
reservations in recruitment and promotions in services and posts; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that seniority of SCs/STs from the date of promotion to next 
grade/post in accordance with the normal rule of seniority is denied in view of the 
Supreme Court's Judgement in R.K. Sabharwal case; 
(d) if so, the steps taken to safeguard the interests of SCs/STs in this regard; and 
(e) whether Government are considering to take up this case for review in Supreme 
Court? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MI NISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Article 16(4) of the Constitution "empowers the State to make any provision for 
the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, 
in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State." 
Article 16 (4A) of the Constitution "empowers the State to make any provision for 
reservation in matters of promotion to any class or classes of posts in the services under the 
State in favour of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes which in the opinion of the 
States, are not adequately represented in the services under the State". 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2000] 
(c) and (d) In R.K. Sabharwal's case the Supreme Court has held that reservation of 
jobs should be related to posts and not to vacancies. In the cases of Virpal Singh Chauhan 
and Ajit singh No. I, the Supreme Court held that accelerated promotion due to rule of 
reservation/roster does not carry with it accel erated consequential seniority. Hence, as 
and when the senior General/ OBC employee is able to catch up with the junior SC/ST 
employee in the immediate higher grade, the former regains his original seniority over 
the latter. In Ajit Singh II, the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court declared that 
above case, have been correctly decided and further held that it is axiomatic in service 
jurisprudence that any promotions made wrongly in excess of any quota are to be treated 
as ad hoc. This applies to reservation quota as much as it applies to direct recruits and 
promotee cases. Thus, while promotion in excess of roster made before 10.2.1995 are 
protected, such promotees cannot claim seniority. 
(e) The review petitions filed against the judgement of the Constitution Bench in Ajit 
Singh II have been dismissed on merits by the Five Judge Bench of the Supreme Court on 
8.12.1999.

Revised guidelines for assistance to NGOs 
3050. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that her Ministry has issued revised guidelines for assisting Non- 
governmental Organisations; 
(b) if so, the details of the revised terms and conditions; and 
(c) how far these guidelines act to promote the sustainable programmes meant for the 
upliftment of targeted people in backward, drought-prone and desertified areas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The salient features of the guidelines are : 
(i) To support projects run by good NGOs working in unserved areas, and to widen 
intervention in the social sector with a view to bring about a healthy sectoral growth in 
areas where little or no attention has been focused so far. 
(ii) To ensure that the spread of assistance is equitably meted out and, keeping in view the 
scarce resources available, encourage the voluntary organizations to mobilize their own 
financial support systems to sustain their activities so that voluntary organizations do 
not solely rely on aid from the government. This will help in ensuring that the limited 
resources available with government are utilized judiciously and as a mean of 
supplementing and not completely funding the voluntary efforts. 
(iii) The Voluntary Organizations should therefore not only be able to sustain their activity 
financially but also be able to involve all resources available to them, including 
community support. 
(iv) In acknowledgement of the need to build up a data base on voluntary activity, the 
guidelines spell out the Ministry's intent to maintain an exclusive data base on Voluntary 
Organisations which would serve as valuable information regarding their capacity, reach, 
area of expertise and involvement as well as their strengths and capacity. 
(v) The mechanism of monitoring and evaluating the performance of the Voluntary 
Organization is sought to be further strengthened and fine tuned. 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2000] 
(vi) In order to ensure transparency, the elected representatives and local 
authorities will be given lists of Voluntary Organizations being financially 
assisted in their areas. 
(vii) Efforts will be made to promote the involvement of qualified and committed 
volunteers who are also professional in their approach. 
(viii) There shall be time bound release of fund and the processing of cases will be 
streamlined in a manner that will reduce unnecessary delay in disposal. 
(c) It is the responsibility of the Ministry to reach the target group which includes the 
Scheduled Castes, Minorities, Backward Classes, Disabled, Aged Persons, Street 
children and victims of Drug Abuse. The objective is to bring them into the mainstream 
of development by assisting them to overcome their social, physical and educational 
handicaps. The guidelines promote and encourage the horizontal spread of development 
alongside sectoral growth in spheres that ha ve received comparatively less attention or 
may need more attention. New projects shall be approved in respect of those voluntary 
organizations which locate these in backwa rd and rural areas wh ich are not benefiting 
from voluntary action at present. New projects will therefore be favoured in rural areas, 
urban areas in cases of extreme need and in States where voluntary action has so far not 
been significant. The areas which are prone to backwardness and natural calamities will 
automatically be covered as new projects in such areas will be given priority whenever a 
sustainable proposal is received.

(b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House {See below)' 
(c) According to the mandate of this Ministry, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the 
nodal Ministry for overall policy, planning & coordination of programmes of development 
for Scheduled Tribes. In regard to the appointment of Scheduled Tribes in services in all 
Government jobs, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the

Statement 
Important observations/recommendation made in the fourth report of National 
Commission for SCs/STs in respect of service safeguards. 
1. The Commission recommends that the whole issue of reservation in services 
should be given a legal basis without any further delay, and the Bill may be 
introduced in the Parliament by the Ministry of Welfare as eraly as possible. The 
Ministry should ensure that penal clause is incorporated in the proposed 
enactment, providing action against offical responsible for deliberate misuse, 
misinterpretation or non-implementation of reservation policy. Alternatively, 
the President may consider issuing an ordinance so that the Constitutional 
safeguards provided to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to have a 
clear, unambiguous legal status. 
2. The Commission, therefore, strongly recommends that Ministry of HRD and 
UGC should take immediate remedial measure and ensure proper 
implementation of the reservation policy by the Universities inlcuding Delhi 
University. 
3. UGC should evaluate the impact of the instructions of 9-10-96 and also that 
the SRDs launched by the Universities. 
4 The Commission feels that such restriction of reservation policy is not order 
and therefore, urges upon the UGC to issue instructions for extending 
reservation in direct recruitment at  all levels including Readers and 
Professors. 
5. All possible steps art therefor, required to be taken to increase the 
representation of SCs/STs in Judicial Services. 
6. The Commission recommends the Department of Personnel and Training 
order deated 29.8.97 should be struck down forthwith. 
7. The Commission recommends that reservation for Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribe in promotion should be extended to all classes 
156 

[21 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of posts in accordance with the spirit of the Constitution (77th Amendment) 
Act. 
8. The Commission recommends that the top administrative authorities should be 
much more vigilant and responsive in this regard to ensure that the Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes employees are not harassed and humiliated in 
any way. 
9. The Commission feels that the Liaison Officers should be provided with all 
possible assistance by the Ministries/Departments/PSEs to enable them to work 
more effectively to ensure adequate representation of SCs/STs in services/posts 
at the earliest. The Department of Personnel & Training should conduct 
orientation training programme for the Liaison Officers as frequently as 
possible.

Pollution in cities due to increase in population 
†3081. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether pollution is increasing in most of cities of the country due to increase in 
the population; 
(b) whether Government have formulated any effective plan or programme to tackle 
this problem; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if no, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) 
Pollution levels exhibit a rising trend in metropolitan towns. This is due to increase in 
economic activities including, industries and transportation, accompanied by growth in 
population. However a decreasing trend has been observed recently in case of National 
Capital Delhi due to various pollution control measures taken by the Government. The 
following steps have been initiated to control pollution in the metropolitan towns: 
(i) Effluent and emission standards have  been notified under the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986 to check pollution. 
(ii) Industries have been directed to install necessary pollution control equipments 
in a time bound basis and legal action is taken against the defaulting units. 
(iii) A scheme under the World Bank for setting up Common Effluent Treatment 
Plants (CETPs) in clusters of small scale industrial units had been taken up. 89 
CETPs have been approved which are at various stages of development. 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2000] 
(iv)  Fiscal incentives are provided for installation of pollution control equipments 
and shifting of industries from congested areas. 
(v)  Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 1994 is in force governing 
environmental appraisal of 29 specified categories of developmental projects. 
(vi)  Environmental Guidelines have been evolved for setting up of industries.  
(vii) Gross, emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emission standards for 
all categories of new vehicles have been notified under the Central Motor 
Vehicles Rules, 1989 and are being enforced by the Department of Transport 
in various urban areas. 
(viii)  For control of pollution from vehicles, emission norms for both petrol and 
diesel driven vehicles at the manufacturing stage were introduced for the first 
time in 1990 and made tighter in 1996. More stringent emission norms have 
come into effect from 1.4.2000. 
(ix)  CNG is supplied for automobiles th rough a number of retail outlets in Delhi 
and Mumbai to cater to the CNG fitted vehicles. 
(x)    All the stone crushers have been closed down in Delhi. 
(xi)  All the Hot Mix Plants and brick kilns have been closed down in Delhi. 
(xii)  A number of hazardous and polluting industries have been closed down in 
Delhi. 
(xiii)  Action Plans for control of pollution in Delhi and Mumbai are being 
implemented. 
(xiv)  24 critically polluted areas have been identified. Action Plans have been 
drawn up for restoration of environmental quality in these areas. 
(xv)  Public awareness campaigns have been launched to educated the people 
about the ill effects of pollution.

Benefits to Employees of Certain Organisations under DRC Act. 
3092. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the employees of the offices like Supreme Court, Election Commission, 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India etc. and other offices which are set up under 
the provisions of Constitution of India, arc covered under Section 14(c) of the Delhi 
Rent Control Act; 
(b) if so, whether these employees are entitled to benefits under Section 14(c) of the 
said Act as are applicable in the case of Central Government employees; 
(c) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a)to(d) 
Section 14Cof the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 gives right to recover immediate 
possession of premises to Central Government employees and Delhi Administration 
employees. The term 'Central Government employees' has not been defined for any 
general purpose. However, as per notification No. 108/54-Ests. (A) dated 20.11.1954 issued 
by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the expression 'Union Government servants' has been 
defined to mean 'all persons whose conditions of service may be regulated by rules made 
by the President under the proviso to article 309 or Clause (5) of article 148 of the 
Constitution'. In view of this definition, the employees of Election Commission, 
Supreme Court, Comptroller and Auditor General of India, etc. and other office which 
are set up under the provisions of the Constitution of India who are covered by the said 
definition, will get protection under Section 14C of Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

Plan for Basic Amenities in Urban Slums at National Level 
3093. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH "SURYA": Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the lack of basic amenities in Urban Slums; 
(b) if so, whether there is any plan for taking care of this at the national level; and 
(c) whether any such plan has been prepared for Delhi in view of the 
regularisation of colonies recently? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) At the national level a scheme known as the National Slum Development 
Programme (NSDP) is already in existance since August, 1996 to provide Additional 
Central Assistance (ACA) to States/UTs for the development of urban slums. The ACA 
released under this scheme can be utilised to provide physical amenities like water 
supply, storm water drains, community infrastructure, community primary health care, 
social amenities like pre-school education, adult education, maternity and child health 
and primary health care etc. it also has a provision for shelter upgradation. 
(c) The Government of NCT of Delhi has adopted the following three pronged strategy 
to deal with Jhuggi Jhopri (JJ) dwellers in the National Capital Territory of Delhi: 
(i) Where the JJ dwellers are residing before 31.1.1990 on land urgently required by the 
land owning agency for the execution of a public purpose project, these JJ dwellers are 
relocated elsewhere, (ii) In-situ upgradation of the JJ colony/cluster is resorted to where 
the land owning agency does not need the land in the foreseeable future and gives NOC 
to the effect that such clusters may be upgraded, (iii) Civic amenities like water supply, 
street lighting, road, storm water drains, etc. are provided in JJ cluster, which do not fall in 
categories (i) and (ii) above. 2. Government  have been issuing instructions to land 
owning agencies from time to time, for taking effective steps to protect their land from 
encroachments etc.

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): Sir, at the 
outset, I would like to assure the hon. Members who have moved the notice for 
discussion on this matter that the Government is well aware of the issues 
concerning jute sector and its importance in our country's economy. The 
Government has been taking various measures in the past not only to protect 
but also to facilitate the growth of this sector. 
Sir, we are keen to ensure that the jute farmers get the maximum 
benefit out of Government's initiatives and interventions. With a view to 
enabling the jute farmers to get remunerative prices of their crop, the 
Government has a Minimum Support Price Policy. The Jute Corporation of 
India, which was established in 1971, implements the same. The MSP for TD 
5/ex Assam during 1998-99 was Rs. 650/- per quintal. The Government 
increased this to Rs. 750/- per quintal in 1999-2000, and further to Rs. 785/- per 
quintal in 2000-01. The JCI has already entered the market and has purchased 
89,000 quintals of raw jute under the MSP so far. The JCI operated 171 centres 
in the jute-growing areas. In addition, the JCI has tied up with the cooperative 
societies and the cooperative organisations of the State Governments to 
increase the coverage of the MSP operations. 
Sir, as the main usage of jute has been in the form of packaging, this 
sector faced rough weather with the emergence of plastic as an alternative 
packaging material in 1980s. Hence, to protect the interests of those engaged in 
this sector, the Government enacted the Jute Packaging Materials Act, 1987 
providing for compulsory use of jute in packaging of certain commodities. 
Orders issued under this Act on 1.7.1999, and modified on 31.3.2000 provided 
for packaging 90 per cent of foodgrains and sugar and 15 per cent of urea in jute 
bags. 
The validity of the order which was to expire on 30th June, 2000 has 
been extended up to 31s1 July, 2000 and then upto 30th September, 2000. The 
Government has not issued any new order for the Jute Year 2000-01. The 
Government intends to issue a new order before 30 th September, 2000 after 
considering various factors like the size of the jute crop, the expected quantity of 
production of foodgrains and sugar, the impact of the introduction of 50 kgs. 
bags in certain sectors etc. Government has been taking a balanced view in the 
matter, considering all

Sir, I hope the Hon'ble Members would agree that the position

THE FOREFEITURE (REPEAL) BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI):  Sir, on behalf of Shri L.K. Advani, my senior colleague, 
I   move: 
That the Bill to repeal the Forfeiture Act, 1859, be taken into 
consideration. 
Sir, this is a very innocuous Bill, just repealing and removing the 
vestiges of the British days, the remnants of the old Act. When there was no 
IPC, when there Was no Cr.PC, when there was no procedure, heinous crimes 
were punished, at that time, by appointment of commissions, and •those 
commissions used to have their own procedure, used to formulate their own 
rules, and would seize, forfeit the properties of the people. As far as I 
understand, Sir, after the 1857 gudder, the revolt of 1857, all these crimes were 
considered heinous and the properties were forfeited. In 1869, some of the 
provisions of the Forfeiture Act were repealed, but still some Sections remained 
to be repealed. We are now proposing to remove all those laws which are just a 
burden on the Statute Book, which are unnecessary. 
The Commission headed by Shri P.C.Jain, which was appointed to 
review  all   Administrative   Laws   and   to   point   out   the   laws   which   are 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [21 AUGUST, 2000] 
unnecessary, also recommended that this Forfeiture Act of 1859 should be 
repeated. By repealing this Act, we will be removing one of the archaic laws and 
we will be taking away the useless burden on the statute book. We will also be 
annihilating the remnants of the old British days. I don't think any of the hon. 
Members present in this august House would like to waste the time of the House 
at this time as the teeth of the original provisions of the Act were removed in 
1869 itself. But provisions which prevented persons who forfeited or ceased of 
holding the properties from going to the civil court or questioning the actions that 
were taken, and all these things remained. By this Forfeiture (Repeal) Bill we 
want to remove these anachronisms and the archaic laws which are in 
existence till today. I hope the House will agree with me and unanimously pass 
this Forfeiture (Repeal) Bill so that we can go ahead and comply with the 
recommendations of the P.C.Jain Commission as also remove the old remnants 
of the British Raj memories.

THE PASSPORT (ENTRY INTO INDIA) AMENDMENT BILL, 2000. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO):   Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 
1920, be taken into consideration. 
Sir, the Indian Passport Act, 1920 provided two provisions, one for 
entry of those who are coming from outside and another for the exit of citizens 
from this country. This Passport Act was amended in 1967 and, at the same 
time, it was renamed as the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920. In the Act of 
1967, for those who contravene the provisions a deterrent punishment was 
provided. But as far as the entry of persons into this country is conerned, the 
penal provisions are meagre. Therefore, it is felt that a deterrent punishment is 
necessary. Therefore, three amendments are proposed. One is to enhance the 
penalty stipulated in sub-section 3 of section 3 of the Passport (Entry into India) 
Act, 1920, that is, to make it "punishable with imprisonment for a term which 
may extend to five years, or with fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees, 
or with both". The second is to incorporate a new section, that is, section 3A, for 
doubling the penalty in the case of second conviction under the Act. 
The third amendment is a minor amendments to Section 4(2) to draw 
reference to Section 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. In the old 
Code of Criminal Procedure, the section in regard to arrest was mentioned in 
section 61. Now it is section 57. With these words, I request the hon. Members 
to pass this Bill.    Thank you. 
The question was proposed.

SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO : Mr. Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, I am thankful to all the Members who have participated in this discussion. 
Most of the Members gave very valid suggestions to effectively deal with the 
provisions of the Passport Act. I am also grateful and thankful to those hon. 
Members who have supported this Bill. Sir, at the outset, I would like to clear 
one point. With regard to the Act, there is some confusion. Sir, the hon. 
Members are aware that entry to India and exit from India are covered by the 
Passport Act of 1920. Subsequently, when it was amended in the yean 967, it 
was decided to bifurcate the Act by providing a separate law for the persons 
exiting from this country. 
So, the Act of 1967 provides for some  rules with regard to those who 
are going out of this country. Consequently, the Passport Act, 1967 was 
enacted. At the same time, the Indian Passport Act, 1920 was renamed as the 
Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920. The 1920 Act was there, and, in the year 
1967, it was renamed as the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920. For exit, there 
is one Act. The same Act has been bifurcated into two, one for exit and the other 
for entry. The Act that provides for the procedure for exit, is having the 
provisions for punishment. A penal punishment, a deterrent punishment, is 
there. If a person goes out of this country with documents that are not valid, he is 
liable to be punished with imprisonment for a period of five years and also 
punished with fine up to Rs.50,ooo/-. But, for those who are entering India, the 
same old punishment is there, which is very lenient. So, it was decided to 
provide for a deterrent punishment for them also, on par with the Act of 1967. 
This is a very, simple thing.

THE BORDER SECURITY FORCE (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI) :   Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I move : 
"That the Bill further to amend the Border Security Force Act, I968, as 
passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, this is a very innocuous, but very beneficial Bill,    with 
far-reaching  consequences  because  the  personnel of the  BSF were  denied 
hitherto the facility of setting off of the period of detention from the punishment. 
This Bill would bring the BSF Act, I968 in tune with the law of the land, as 
contained in section 428 of the Cr.P.C. The BSF personnel were not availing of 
this facility so far which was already available to the civilians under section 428 
of the Criminal Procedure Code and which was also .available to the Army 
personnel under section I69 of the Army Act. This provision is also in existence 
for the ITBP personnel, for the CISF personnel and for the general civilians also. 
So, by this Bill, it is proposed to amend the BSF Act, I968, with a view to 
inserting a new clause, a new provision, in the BSF Act on the lines of section 
I69A of the Army Act and section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code, I973 so 
as to provide for setting off of the period of pre-trial detention against the 
sentence of imprisonment imposed on a person governed by the Border 
Security Force Act, I968, and the Bill seeks to achieve this aforesaid object. By 
this, it will also safeguard the legal rights of the BSF personnel facing trial which 
the citizens of the country  are already enjoying. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [21 AUGUST, 2000] 
Incidentally, the Supreme Court also, in its judgement in I996, has held 
that section 428 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not apply to the BSF 
people. The Army Act has its own provision; civilians also enjoy that benefit 
under the normal law of the land. So, that beneficial provision is there in the 
Cr.P.C. This was missing so far in the BSF Act. The Supreme Court has also 
made an observation in its judgement in the case of Union of India versus Anand 
Singh Bisht wherein they pointed out that such a provision should be made. So, 
this Bill is being placed before this august House for consideration and passing.

SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI (Tamil Nadu) : Sir, the Border 
Security Force (Amendment) Bill that is brought before us is going to provide a 
facility to the BSF personnel, that is, the period of custody undergone by a BSF 
person, if a Security Force Court convicts him, has to be set off against the 
period of sentence imposed upon him. 
Sir, I take this opportunity to highlight some very important issues that 
are faced or confronted by the BSF. Sir, you know insurgency is there in eleven 
States in India. Therefore, the job of the BSF is very hazardous. Previously, they 
had to consider only the climatic conditions. Now, the cross-border terrorism 
makes the public hesitant to join the BSF. That is the situation. Therefore, the 
facilities that are extended to the BSF should be such that they should be 
welcomed by one and all. During the Kargil stand-off an important matter was 
published in the Press that the BSF people, who were working there, were 
suffering from swollen feet or ulcer caused by perspiration due to woollen socks. 
This is due to perspiration in-betweer> the legs and the socks. Now, a new 
invention has taken place in Germany. They are manufacturing some kind of 
socks which will provide you protection but, at the same time, there will be no 
perspiration. The Government of Pakistan had purchased this kind of socks and 
issued them to the people who were crossing into India. I request the 
Government to verify this info rmation. If it is correct, we have to take it up with 
the German Government and see that the same quality socks are being 
purchased and provided to our BSF people as also Defence people. This is 
number one. 
The BSF is interconnected with the defence.  In the Defence

THE CABLE TELEVISION NETWORKS (REGULATION) 
AMENDMENT BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Cable Television Networks 
(Regulation) Act, 1995, as passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, this was an Act intended to regulate the cable network system 
within India. At the time when this Act was adopted and put into implementation, 
perhaps, we did not have sufficient experience because, at that time, this 
industry in India was nascent. Now, for the last five - six years, after seeing the 
functioning of this Act, there are a few amendments which have been 
necessitated. Probably, these amendments are in three -four categories. I will 
just specify each one of them. The' main amendment being that, in section 5 
and section 6 of the original Act, there was a provision for a broadcasting code 
and an advertising code, to be provided 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [21 AUGUST, 2000] 
for under the provisions of this Act, However, in both the sections, even though 
the rules provided for the broadcasting code and the advertising code, there 
was a proviso that this would apply only to channels which are incripted and 
those which are free to air would be exempted from the provisions of the Act. 
[The Vice-Chairman (Shri Adhik  Shirodkar) in the Chair] 
So, two categories of channels have been operating-one for which 
some money has to be paid, which are known as pay channels or encripted 
channels, which are telecast with the help of a decoder. The broadcasting code 
and the advertising code lay down various norms on advertising and 
broadcasting of programmes. We found that the programmes which were free 
to air were exempted from the broadcasting code and the advertising code. As a 
result of which, several complaints used to be received. On several occasions, 
in this House itself, hon. Members had occasions to point out this anomaly 
which existed in the Act. Therefore, an amendment has been proposed to 
section 5 and section 6. The proviso to section 5 and 6 are sought to be deleted 
now. The boradcasting code and the advertisement code would be applicable to 
all channels which are carried to our homes by the cable operators. 
The second amendment which has been proposed is, to implement 
this Act, certain officers have to be notified by the Central Government. But 
since officers were to operate at the level of every district in the country, since 
cable operation is operated at the very grassroot level in every city and district of 
the country, there was a difficulty in having officers nominated by the Central 
Government in each of the areas. Hence, the States were requested to 
nominate the officers; but several States, in fact, found it difficult even to 
nominate the officers. Therefore, amendments are proposed so that the Act 
itself would prescribe who the officers would be. The District Magistrate of every 
district, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate and the Commissioner of Police of every 
area would be the authorised officers who would really have to implement the 
provisions of this Act. 
Sir, the third amendment re^s to the carrying of channels of 
Doordarshan. There is a 'must carry' clause, which exists in section 8 of the Act. 
Section 8 provides that at least two Doordarshan channels would be carried on 
every cable network. Now, our experience has shown that in a 
256 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
large number of places, either this was not being done or was done in a manner 
that the signals were not being well received from the cable operators. Satellite 
signals and terrestrial signals were mixed with each other. A provision has now 
been made that every cable operator would telecast at least two terrestrial 
channels, and one regional language channel too would be shown on the prime 
band. As you see, Doordarshan, in the last one year, has started a large number 
of regional language satellite channels in every State language, in almost every 
regional language. Therefore, there is a 'must carry' clause in this Bill. In fact, 
the Standing Committee had recommended that the Act be amended so as to 
see that these provisions are really, adequately, enforced. 
Sir, the last amendment is to section 20, which is now sought to be 
substituted. Section 19 originally dealt with prohibition on individual 
programmes. Certain conditions were prescribed. Section 20 has a larger 
prohibition; the Central Government has the power to provide a prohibition with 
regard to certain cable networks. We have, therefore, provided certain 
categories where there are programmes which are detrimental to the public 
interest, on several ponsiderations; and, there is a power which is given in 
section 20, saying that those networks can be prohibited, after a hearing being 
given to them. The conditions under which they can be prohibited are the same 
which are there in article 19(2). They have been verbally lifted from there. 
Whatever are the Constitutionally-prescribed limitations on freedom of 
expression, which the Constitution haslaid down in article 19(2), have been put 
in section 20 of this Bill. 
These are the four categories of amendments which we have 
proposed to this Act. I, therefore, propose that this hon. House take this Bill into 
consideration and pa'ss this amendment to the 1995 Act. 
Thank you.

SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD (Bihar): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am 
extremely grateful that you have given me an opportunity to speak on this Bill. I 
wholeheartedly support this Bill. The cable revolution is a part of our daily life 
today. We cannot wish it away. Operators have got the right to show; people 
have got the right to see. But, obviously, it is not unlimited. That is why in the 
year 1955, a regulatory mechanism was introduced there. It was a welcome 
development. With the passage of time, certain missing links were felt, and it is 
very heartening to note that those missing links are sought to be filled up by 
today's amendment. Of particular relevance is the amendment to sections 5 and 
6 of the parent Act. There are two provisos - in section 5, if a foreign TV channel 
did not confirm to the programme code, there was no control; similarly, in 
section 6, if the advertisement that is telecast by the foreign channels did not 
confirm to the advertisement code, there was an exemption; there was no need 
for that. We have civilizational norms. There has been a consensus in the 
country about certain behavioural norms by which we seek to undertake our 
social intercourse. And if the foreign channels are not susceptible to those 
feelings of this country, the exemption that was available to them under sections 
5 and 6 has to go. My dear colleague, Shri Pachouri, mentioned about certain 
channels. I don't want to name any particular channel. But I would certainly 
request the hon. Minister to do something in regard to the reckless manner in 
which some of the presentations are being made by many of the foreign 
channels, in complete disregard of the social norms of this country. Certainly, 
creative freedom ought to be recognised. Certainly, creativity ought to be given 
due respect. But there is also an equally important element of the susceptibility 
of the society in which it is sought to be presented.We need not always go by the 
rigid modalities of this

discussion, but certainly if there is a consensus that a particular advertisement 
or a programme is transcending that norm, the law will have to intervene. Sir, I 
have an example of a particular advertisement where a television company

manner in order to sell its television. Certainly, it is blasphemy in the extreme. I 
am happy to learn that a protest was made, and now a control has been 
brought. Therefore, the renewal of the exemption in sections 5 and 6, which was 
available to the foreign satellite channels, is a very welcome development. 
Sir, as far as the amendment to section 8 is concerned, making it 
obligatory upon the cable operators to show two terrestrial channel 
programmes and a local language programme, is equally welcome. Since there 
is a cable revolution today, the people of the country in a particular State have

children, which we have seen over the years. Therefore, I feel it is a very 
welcome development, as far as the amendment to section 8 is concerned, 
because it has now been made obligatory, while in the parent Act, they had a 
right to choose that. Equally welcome, Sir, is the amendment to section 11, 
because initially the bar was, if it was not registered, it could be confiscated. 
Now if it is in violation of sections 5,6,7 and 8, even then the power of seizure 
has been given. 
Lastly, I would like to make few observations about the amendment to

respectfully that people also have got a right to be appreciated about their 
sentiments. A mean, a balance has to be struck, and I think there is also a 
general consensus in the country.   If this balance is kept in mind, I am sure the

SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nominated): I will do it in one-and-a-half 
minutes. I would specifically refer to Clause 9 of the Bill which says, "Section 20 of the 
principal Act shall be re-numbered as sub-section (1) thereof and after sub-section 
(1) as so re-numbered... There can be no two opinions that the sovereignty, integrity 
and security of India are supreme and should never be compromised. However, no 
Government agency should be allowed to hide its administrative failures or 
excesses or atrocities behind these respectable terms. I would like to refer to 
clause 9 (iii) If a friendly State commits atrocities on its citizens or minorities, should we 
be disallowed from commenting on it? 
In recent times, we had seen rising racial intolerance in Great Britain, 
where the Asians of Indian origin have been victimised. Surely we have the legitimate 
right to register our protest. In the past, we have gone all out in support of a 
Bangladeshi writer who was exiled from her country having earned the ire of religious 
fundamentalists by boldly exposing them in her novel. Surely we cannot jettison our 
right to do so in the interest of friendly relations of India with any foreign State. 
Now I come to the most contentious sub-clause 3. The important point is: 
What body of people in the Central Government is going to define public order 
decency or morality? I respectfully submit that it is not the Government's business to 
define decency and morality. Governments come and go. Their codes of decency and 
morality are governed by their political ideology. Does that mean that the people of 
India must accept a new code of morality every five years, that is if the Government is 
lucky enough to last its full term? We only need to look at the map of the world or 
trace history to know that whenever Governments have been allowed to take on the 
mantle of morality, they have ended up curbing civil liberties and, more often than not, 
the voice of the weaker sections. 
281 

RAJYA SABHA [21 AUGUST, 2000] 
The film industry in India is already suffering because of being 
subjected to the Censor Board that is accused of being both whimsical ar 
arbitrary. In fact, there is a great demand from within the industry that the 
Government should do away with the Censor Board altogether, -- we are still 
following the archaic British system -- that the American model is a better 
example. There, the filmmakers themselves subject their films to a grading 
system. Not a single cut is made but vulnerable sections such as children are 
protected from excessive sex and violence by grades with the help of adults, 
parents,   etc. 
If the Government is allowed to decide issues like decency and 
morality, then it will lead to a rigid adherence of the status quo - women 
challenging the system, the voice of minorities, the voice of the weaker sections 
gain strength by striking against the anvil of status quo and creating sparks. In a 
democracy, we are committed to protecting these freedoms. 
In the past, - I think it was in 1993 - there was the horrific instance of 
self-styled morality of the leaders of the BJP dictating to the film industry as to 
what can or cannot be allowed in films, and this in spite of the already existing 
Censor Board. And it is a matter of deep anguish to me that even today the film 
industry is being forced to tamely agree to these conditions The Shiv Sena went 
a step further. They said that since Mr. A.K. Hangal had attended the Pakistan 
National Day, he should not be allowed to work in Hindi films, though it was a 
fact that a very senior leader of the BJP Government was also happily seen on 
the occasion. It did not suit the Shiv Sena. So it was not mentioned. But Mr. A. K. 
Hangal was subjected to this. And it is a matter of great shame that the film 
industry was forced to cut him out of films, films that were new, plus the films that 
he has already worked in. 
SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI: Before we start accusing the producers 
of being spineless, we also need to understand that in the absence of the State 
being able to deliver compensation or justice to the beleaguered producer, he is 
left with no option but to succumb to such pressures.   The fear psychosis that 
can be created in such ah atmosphere 
282 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA  
leads to the stifling of creative freedom and this cannot augur well for a 
democracy. 
Our recent history has been scarred by extra-constitutional attacks on 
freedom of expression. Films have been pulled out of theatres; shooting of 
legitimately cleared films have been stopped; running plays have been forced to 
shut down; there are numerous instances. Each time they have acted to curb 
the freedom of expression which is the hallmark of a true democracy. 
Defining the decency or morality of a society is not the business of the 
Government. This can only be decided by a group of intellectuals drawn from all 
sections of society, free from the political ideology of the Government of the 
day, functioning as a completely autonomous body. 
If the basic purpose of sub-clause 2 is truly what it claims to be and not 
to further a hidden agenda, then it must also state that an autonomous body, 
drawn from all sections of society, will be constituted to look into the aspects of 
decency or morality. I respectfully request the hon. Minister to issue a 
clarification in this regard.   Thank you.

There have been, however, issues and questions which have been raised and I 
think it is important that those queries or words of caution are also dealt with. Let 
me, in the first instance, say that as far as television industry in India is 
concerned, which most of us see through the instrumentality of the cable 
operators it does not provide for any form of pre-censorship. What is shown on 
television is subject to a code which the law has regulated, the broadcasting 
code and the advertising code. We leave it to our programmers and our channel 
operators and cable operators to abide by that code. If anyone of them violates

really a censorship law. We are laying down the norm on the basis of which this 
cable industry and channel industry really is to be operated. There are several 
provisions which have been made in this Bill and as far as the first and most 
important provision is concerned, we have deleted the proviso to Section 5 and 
Section 6. I am grateful that no Member really has said, 'there must be this kind 
of discrimination which should go on, that only some channels must be

are working with the State Governments, under the jurisdiction of the State 
Governments. We have not taken away any powers of the State Governments. You 
also mentioned, and very rightly so, that in some States, there is no Commissioner 
of Police. You may have to nominate a Superintendent of Police or a Director-General 
of Police. The amendment to the Act further says that we are entitled to notify in 
the Official Gazette such other names or designations of officers who will further be 
entitled to really put this Act into operation. So, that provision has also been kept, as 
far as this Act is concerned. As far as section 5 is concerned, with regard to the 
must carry clause', and I must say, Sir, that there is a history behind these 'must 
carry clauses', these 'must carry clauses' are really there in a large number of 
jurisdictions in India and outside. Even in the original section 8, there was a 'must 
carry clause' that two channels of Doordarshan must be carried. The rationale 
behind this 'must carry clause' is that there are some channels which function in public 
interest; for instance, the object of Doordarshan is tht it is to be a public service 
broadcaster. Then, these are programmes which the cable operators, when they 
bring to the houses, must really mandatorily show. In the last year or so - an effort had 
been made even earlier - Doordarshan has succeeded in launching a number of 
satellite channels in regional languages. So, we have stated that two plus one of 
these cable channels must necessarily be shown on the prime band. There are 
countries where there are children's channels, health channels, educational channels.   
Now, 
292 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
a question was raised by several Members: What about an educational 
channel? On the 26th of January this year, the HRD Ministry and the Prasar 
Bharti started a programme, named Gyandarshan. We have some UGC 
courses on the national channel. It is a channel which is exclusively an 
educational channel. It is India's first educational channel. This educational 
channel has very good quality programmes that are produced by the Indira 
Gandhi National Open University. But, unfortunately, most of the cable 
operators are not carrying it, Therefore, with regard to the educational channel - 
or tomorrow, you may have a children's channel --should it not be mandatorily 
obligatory - because there is a section of the population which needs this, and 
we must encourage these channels -- that there must be a 'must carry clause'? 
For instance, in the United States, the children's channel is a mandatory 
channel. Each cable operator has to carry it because it caters to a segment of 
the audience, which must receive the kind of programme that it is entitled to. 
Several other questions were also raised here. But I must come now to the issue 
raised by Shabanaji and Shri Kuldip Nayyar with regard to the amendments 
made to section 20 of this Act. I must say that the fears which you have 
expressed are really not real for the reason that we are in the 50th year of our 
republic, and amongst the provisions of the Constitution which we have worked 
and worked very well, is article 19 under the Fundamental Rights. Article 19 
gives us the freedom of expression, and, therefore, somebody in print media, or 
somebody in electronic media, may use this freedom of expression really to 
voice what he wants to say. Or somebody may use it for political expression. 
Now what should be the parameters of restriction on this free expression? That 
is the only question. These are not phrases which we have invented today, in the 
year 2000. These are the phrases which were there in the draft Constitution, and 
which were approved by the Constituent Assembly. There are several other 
Fundamental Rights where there is a 'general phrase'. You can have a 
reasonable restriction on the Fundamental Rights. But as far as freedom of 
expression is concerned, such a general phrase was discouraged. In article 
19(2) a provision was made that the only restriction on free expression will not 
be a restriction which is per se reasonable because the concept of 
reasonableness can vary from person to person. 
But the six or seven areas which were defined were: the sovereignty 
and integrity of India; the security of the State; friendly relations with foreign 
States;    public order, decency or morality, or in relation to 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [21 AUGUST, 2000] 
contempt of court, defamation or incitement of an offence. Now what we have 
really done in section 20 is that we have bodily lifted the provisions which the 
farmers of India's Constitution formulated. Shri Kuldip Nayyar said, 'What is 
public order? It is an undefined concept.' Well, public order is a phrase which we 
have bodily lifted from the Constitution itself, as a reasonable restriction. Now, 
'public order', though it was mentioned as an expression, in the Constitution, 
fortunately, in the last 50 years, it has got a very well-defined judicial meaning 
and nobody can really go beyond that judicial meaning. If some Government of 
the day tried to go beyond that judicial meaning - we have a very independent 
judiciary; judicial review is available - certainly, the courts have stepped in the 
past when free expression has been taken away for reasons other than public 
order, which are attributable to public order. For example, let me take an 
illustration which would have been very close to his heart if he was present. A 
channel incites caste hatred, or, a channel incites religious animosity. And it is a 
round-the-clock channel which does that. But for this provision of 'public order', 
there would be no other power available to the Government to step in and say 
this is a threat to public order, and therefore, we step in to stop this. You are right 
that an expression like 'public order' should not be used merely because there is 
criticism of Governments or there is somebody hostile to you. The existence of 
the power is entirely different from the misuse or the abuse of that power. The 
existence of this power in section 20 is absolutely necessary. It is only the abuse 
which has to be avoided. If and when an abuse does take place, there are other 
mechanisms within the system which are competent and strong enough, 
constitutionally empowered and ready to take action against that. Shabana ji 
mentioned about friendly relations of India with any foreign State. We are an 
open and an independent society. We allow criticism. We also criticize, our 
citizens criticize, our newspapers criticize, foreign states which may be friendly 
to us. We don't have a single precedent of the Government of having stepped in 
to stop that. But there may be extreme illustrations which take place, where 
some countries are used as hubs to launch activities of a particular kind and 
which may be cetrimental to diplomatic relations. It is only in those extreme 
cases that the Constitution has empowered the State; in terms of article 19(2), at 
that stage you can step in and say that this is creating a great diplomatic 
embarrassment to this country. We cannot allow a group of citizens to go to that 
extent. Fortunately, there are very rare, almost negligible instances, in the last 
50 years, of this power ever having been used.   I am reasonably confident that 
294 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
such situation will not arise in future. But the existence of the power is purely in 
consonance with what the Constitution itself has provided. You are right when 
you say that concepts of decency and morality must not change from time to 
time when Governments change. The Government is a continuing entity. It is 
individual and political parties which come and go. And, therefore, when 
individuals and political parties come and go, they cannot substitute their own 
assessments really to say what should be allowed and what should not be 
allowed. Therefore, we cannot really have any kind of standards at one given 
time to be defined, which should prescribe this. But again, it is these phrases. 
Now, if we saw the concern of the House, most Members have been, in fact, 
very assertive in saying "why do we allow programmes which destroy the 
cultural heritage of this country and which are indoctrinating our people, in 
terms of, let us say, a certain extreme example of fashion which borders on 
obscenity or in cases where family break-ups are eulogised, extra-marital 
relationships are eulogised, etc. So, these are all illustrations people have 
given. Therefore, in section 20, the words used are 'decency and morality', 
which is really an assessment. I agree with you, there may be, at times, 
difficulties in individuals defining these phrases. But then, again, it is only when 
somebody crosses the line, that is, the line of acceptability in a society, that the 
State steps in. For example, in the existing Act, as it originally was, in section 
20, the position existent was far worse. The original section 20 read, ' If the 
Central Government thinks it is necessary in public interest to prohibit a 
channel...'. So, the condition precedent was, 'the existence of public interest'. 
Now, 'public interest' is a meaning which could have been stretched. We have 
now narrowed that 'public interest' to only mean the Constitutionally permissible 
restrictions. 
Sir, we have defined those restrictions. Therefore, instead of giving a 
very broad power which is capable of misuse, we have now defined it in these 
four or five words which we have used here, that, it is only in these five 
contingencies that you can step in and prohibit something. For instance, I must 
tell you that we are always continuously thinking as to what are those areas 
where we receive a large number of complaints. We receive complaints against 
programmes, we receive complaints against channels and we receive 
complaints against individual advertisements. Our effort is that we must try and 
caution people who know as to what the broadcasting code is, what the 
advertisement code is, that they have to 
295 

RAJYA SABHA (21 AUGUST, 2000) 
abide by; and once they fall in line, it is not a very happy occasion for the 
Government to pass prohibitory orders. The only prohibitory order that we have 
passed under this Act is against a channel which past midnight was showing 
purely pornographic programmes, and it was prohibited sometime in the month 
of October last year. So, except that one extreme case where hard pornography 
was being shown, we have tried to caution people. Most people are now abiding

well. However, as far as a large number of regional channels is concerned, 
there is still a scope for improvement, and I am sure, they will certainly take note 
of it. Sir, a number of other suggestions which were made related to the overall 
quality of programmes which one telecast on various channels. We have taken 
note of all those valuable suggestions which have been made. Certainly, the 
advertising code and the broadcasting code, which are part of the rules which 
have been framed under this Act, are wide enough to take care of a large 
number of those suggestions. Hopefully, once this Act is put into 
implementation, the compliance of these codes by all channels, including the 
'free to air' channels, would also be possible.   I am extremely grateful to you, 
Sir, for 
296 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
having given me this opportunity.   I am also grateful to the hon. Members who 
have made very valuable suggestions.

BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL) :   Sir, I move: 
That the Bill further to amend the State Financial Corporations Act,

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR): Mr. Minister, do

SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL: Hon. Vice-Chairman, Sir, the 
existing State. Financial Corporation Act was enacted almost five decades ago. 
At present, 18 State Financial Corporations are functioning in various States.   
These SFCs have played an important role in evolution and growth 
298 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of small and medium scale industries. However, with the changing business 
environment, the SFCs have started facing a number of problems relating to 
organisational structure, management, resource mobilisation, operational 
efficiency, overall financial health etc. 
To enable the SFCs to adapt themselves to the emerging environment 
and enhance their ability to respond to the needs of the changing financial 
system, it has become imperative to enlarge their shareholder base and provide 
them with a greater functional autonomy and operational flexibility. This has 
necessitated comprehensive amendments to the State Financial Corporations 
Act. The main features of the proposed amendments are: 
• Transfer of the IDBI shareholdings in the SFCs in favour of the 
SIDBI; 
• Capital restructuring of the State Financial Corporations with, a 
view to increase the authorised share capital, enlarge shareholder 
base, permit issue of share capital up to forty-nine per cent to the 
public and to allow the Financial Corporations to reduce or convert 
the existing share capital; 
• Providing full security to the SFCs with regard to borrowing, 
acceptance of the deposits and investment of surplus funds; 
• Restructuring of the Board of Directors of SFCs and vesting 
greater powers in the General Body of Shareholders for 
appointment of Auditors, approval of rate of dividend and approval 
of annual accounts. 
Sir, strengthening of the SFCs would go a long way in promotion and 
development of small and medium scale industry in the country. 
Sir, I commend this Bill, as passed by Lok Sabha, for its consideration 
and for being passed. 
The question was proposed. 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN (Karnataka):    Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I
