welcome the Bill to amend the State Financial Corporations Act. Sir, this Bill was 
long overdue. In fact, we are discussing this Amendment to the State Financial 
Corporation Act, when the small and medium scale industries in the entire 
country are facing difficulties. 
The small and medium scale industries have played a very vital role in 
the Indian economy. The State Financial Corporations have also played a very 
dynamic role in promoting the small-scale industries in the country. 
But, Sir, today's scenario is quite different. The small-scale industries 
almost all over the country are facing difficulties. 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Figures di ffer. Some reports say nearly 
40-45 per cent of the small-scale industries are at the closure stage. In the case 
of some of them it may be because of administrative lapses or because of those 
people who have not been able to raise these industries properly. But, today, 
the small-scale industries are suffering mainly because of unequal competition 
and liberal imports. From 1992 onwards, the Government started thinking of 
various changes in the State Financial Corporations Act. Under section 4 of the 
Act, an effort is being made to expand the activities of the small-scale industries. 
It has now been suggested in the Bill to include several other activities like 
providing finances to management services, financial services, health services, 
software and hardware technology, telecommunications, providing commercial 
complex facilities and so on. While doing this, we have to be very careful. For 
example, take the construction industry. What type of construction activities 
should we include? Then there are similar other activities. While you define the 
industry, you have to consider the area of their activities as well. 
Financial Corporations are established to promote small-scale and 
medium-scale industries, which will simultaneously generate employment 
oppurtunities. There are certain activities included in Section 4 of the Act, which 
will not help in creation of employment opportunities. If a lot of finances go to 
such activities, they will not generate employment. We should be careful on this 
aspect. Small-scale industries have played a great role in creating employment 
opportunities as well as self-employment opportunities. 
Another important thing in this Bill is the question of raising capital. 
300 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
I welcome this, because the State Financial Corporations through this Bill are 
given power to raise capital. So far, the captial for the Financial Corporations 
was being contributed either through the State Governments or through the 
national financial institutions or through the IDBI. Now, SIDBI is being brought in 
as a monitoring agency, instead of IDBI. Earlier various other financial 
institutions used to contribute to the State Financial Corporations. 
Now, this Bill authorises the State Financial Corporations to raise 
capital, up to 49 per cent, from the market, in addition to from the State 
Government, other financial institutions and from the SIDBI. As a result, the 
State Financial Corporations will become more competitive. They will have to 
be made more accountable. The State Financial Corporations by going to the 
public for raising capital, are making themselves more accountable. This is the 
best thing. Up till now, they were not made strictly accountable because they 
were accountable to the Government or to some financial institution. But now 
they will be subjected to public scrutiny because public will be investing in their 
capital. This is also a welcome change. Then, I would like to seek one 
clarification from the hon. Minister. Now there is a provision in the Bill to reduce 
the capital. Section 4E states, "The Financial Corporation, with the prior 
approval of the State Government and the Small Industries Bank, may, by 
resolution passed in a general meeting of the shareholders, reduce its share 
capital in any way." When you are talking of increasing the share capital, .why 
should there be a provision for reducing the share capital? I would like to know 
from the hon. Minister as to why such a provision is there. 
Sir, while appreciating the various measures which have been 
brought in by the Government, I would like to point out that all is not well with the 
managements of the State Financial Corporations. We have seen that there is a 
lot of red-tapism in the State Financial Corporations. If a small-scale unit 
submits a proposal for sanctioning of a loan, the proposal may take one or two 
years. The proposals are not considered. Time is the essence in an industry. As 
a result of this, there is no transparency. We are living in an era of transparency. 
There should be accountability on the part of financial institutions or on the part 
of the State Financial Corporations to sanction loans before a certain time. A 
timeframe should be fixed. 
In fact, there are several articles published on the functioning of the 
301 

RAJYA SABHA [21 AUGUST, 2000] 
State Financial Corporations wherein it has been clearly stated that the State 
Financial Corporations should be able to give their consent for financing a 
project within a certain time; a time-limit should be fixed, say, 30 days or 40 days 
or 50 days. They can do it, possibly through a good and integrated data system. 
For instance, if a borrower approaches a State Financial Corporation for setting 
up an industry, for a specific project with a specific installed capacity and 
location of a project, the SFC should be in a position to say, by having a proper 
data, that they are going to sanction the loan by such and such time. Now, there 
is a lot of red-tapism. Regarding the sanctioning of loans, I would not like to go 
into the details. My point is transparency has to be brought in while processing a 
loan application and in sanctioning of it. 
Another important thing which has probably escaped attention is 
section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act wherein they have been given 
the power to take over a unit if it defaults in payment. When you recover the 
loan, you have to be firm in recovering the loan. We agree with that. Now, 
section 29 gives a power to the State Financial Corporation to take over a unit if 
it defaults in payment. Under section 29, a number of instances are there where 
a running unit has been taken over because of default in payment and the unit 
will suffer and will be almost killed. They will not take action immediately. When 
the unit is taken, if you want to sell it, you will not realise anything. You will have 
to sell it at a throw-away price. Sometimes, they take over a unit, lock it and keep 
it for one year. The unit will lose its value. Its market is lost. I am not saying, for a 
moment, that you should dilute the powers of the State Financial Corporation as 
far as the recovery measures are concerned. In fact, this matter has been dealt 
with by the Supreme Court also. The Supreme Court has given certain 
guidelines as to the use of section 29, what should be the various constraints. 
interruption). Constraint is there on me also. However, I would like to bring them 
to the notice of the hon. Minister. You should consider bringing certain 
amendments to the use of section 29. Even some articles have called it a 
draconian law. The Supreme Court, in Mahesh Chandra v. Regional Manager, 
UPFC, has formulated certain guidelines as to how it should be included. There 
is a complaint that while dealing with recovery under section 29, because of the 
misuse of section 29, industries have suffered. I would like to request the hon. 
Minister to look into this issue. 
Then, there is a need for a comprehensive law. These amendments

passed the Bill and the Bill is a progressive Bill. But there is a need for a

I once again welcome this Bill and I hope the hon. Minister will
